record.title: Monthly high-dose cholecalciferol and falls in older care-home residents: a double-blind randomised trial
record.abstract: Background: Falls are common among older people living in residential care, and vitamin D insufficiency is widespread in this group. Whether monthly high-dose supplementation reduces falls is uncertain. Methods: We randomised 684 residents aged 70 years or older from 41 care homes to 60,000 IU cholecalciferol or identical placebo capsules given monthly for 12 months. Residents with a history of kidney stones or hypercalcaemia were excluded. Care staff recorded falls prospectively in daily diaries using a standard definition; residents, care staff and investigators were blinded to allocation. The primary outcome was the rate of falls. Results: 642 residents (94%) completed follow-up. The rate of falls was 1.9 per person-year in the vitamin D group and 2.1 in the placebo group (rate ratio 0.91, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.06). Fractures were infrequent in both groups. Hypercalcaemia occurred in three participants in the vitamin D group and one in the placebo group. Conclusions: Monthly high-dose vitamin D did not significantly reduce falls among care-home residents. Funding: Regional Health Research Fund (fictional); capsules supplied by the manufacturer, which had no role in the analysis.
record.discussion_excerpt: Our population differs from community-dwelling older adults in several ways. Care-home residents are frailer, more often cognitively impaired, and more likely to be vitamin D deficient at baseline; they also have more supervised mobility and different fall hazards. Earlier community trials used daily rather than monthly dosing. We therefore caution against extrapolating our null result to people living independently, while noting that the direction of effect was similar to that of recent community trials.

Title: Introducing a sepsis recognition bundle across hospital wards: a stepped-wedge cluster randomised trial

Abstract: Background: Delayed recognition of sepsis on general wards contributes to preventable deaths. Methods: Sixteen general medical and surgical wards in four hospitals were randomised to the order in which they crossed from usual care to a sepsis recognition bundle (electronic early-warning score with automated alerts, nurse education and a rapid-response escalation pathway). Every four months, four further wards crossed over, until all wards had the bundle. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality among patients with suspected sepsis; secondary outcomes were time to antibiotics and ICU admission. Analysis used mixed models adjusting for calendar time. Results: 9,412 patient episodes with suspected sepsis were included. Time to antibiotics was shorter under the bundle. In-hospital mortality was lower under the bundle, but the difference was not statistically significant after adjustment for time trends. Conclusions: The bundle shortened time to antibiotics; its effect on mortality is uncertain.

record.title: Acupressure wristbands for postoperative nausea after laparoscopic surgery: randomised sham-controlled trial
record.methods: Adults undergoing elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy at two hospitals were randomised by a telephone service, using computer-generated blocks of variable size, to acupressure wristbands placed at the P6 point or to sham wristbands placed at a non-acupoint on the dorsal wrist. Bands were applied by theatre nurses in the anaesthetic room after induction. Patients were told they would receive 'one of two wristband positions being studied'. The primary outcome was patient-reported nausea severity on a 0-10 scale at 2, 6 and 24 hours after surgery, collected by ward nurses who were not told the allocation but could see the band position. Vomiting episodes and rescue antiemetic use were taken from the drug chart. All patients received standard antiemetic prophylaxis. Before discharge, patients were asked which band they thought they had received; 41% of the acupressure group and 38% of the sham group guessed 'real acupressure', and the rest guessed sham or did not know.
record.results: Of 260 randomised patients, 254 were analysed (intervention 127, sham 127); six were excluded after conversion to open surgery. Mean nausea scores were lower with acupressure at 6 hours (difference -0.9 points, 95% CI -1.6 to -0.2) but not at 2 or 24 hours. Rescue antiemetic use was similar between groups. No adverse events related to the bands were reported. Two patients in each group removed their bands early because of skin irritation; their data were retained in the analysis.
record.registration: Prospectively registered; the registry lists nausea at 6 hours as the primary time point, with 2 and 24 hours as secondary.
record.funding: No external funding. The wristband manufacturer supplied bands free of charge and had no other role.
record.discussion_excerpt: The benefit at 6 hours was modest and did not translate into reduced rescue antiemetic use. The blinding check suggests patients could not reliably tell which band they wore. We did not record whether ward nurses recognised the P6 position.

record.title: Lung ultrasound for pneumonia in the emergency department: a diagnostic accuracy study
record.abstract: Methods: We recruited 150 adults with pneumonia confirmed on chest CT from the inpatient wards and 150 healthy volunteers from hospital staff. Emergency physicians with at least two years of ultrasound experience performed lung ultrasound and recorded their interpretation before seeing any imaging results. The reference standard was chest CT for patients; volunteers did not undergo CT and were classified as disease-free. Results: Sensitivity was 96% and specificity 98%. Conclusions: Lung ultrasound is highly accurate for pneumonia in emergency settings.
record.methods_excerpt: Chest CT scans for the patient group had been performed as part of routine care before study enrolment and were reported by the duty radiologist. Ultrasound examinations were performed at the bedside on the wards, typically two to four days after admission, when most patients had started antibiotics. Healthy volunteers were scanned in a staff room during working hours. Ultrasound findings were classified as positive if consolidation or focal B-lines were present.

record.title: Oral anticoagulant ZX-44 versus warfarin in atrial fibrillation: the ZEPHYR-AF randomised trial
record.abstract: Methods: 6,200 patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation were randomised in a double-blind, double-dummy design to ZX-44 (a fictional factor Xa inhibitor) or dose-adjusted warfarin. The primary efficacy outcome was stroke or systemic embolism; the primary safety outcome was major bleeding. Results: Stroke or systemic embolism occurred in 1.5% per year with ZX-44 and 1.7% per year with warfarin (non-inferiority met). Major bleeding occurred in 2.1% and 3.0% per year respectively. Intracranial haemorrhage was less frequent with ZX-44. Gastrointestinal bleeding was 'similar'. Conclusions: ZX-44 was non-inferior to warfarin and caused less major bleeding.
record.registry_outcomes: Registered secondary safety outcomes: major bleeding; clinically relevant non-major bleeding; intracranial haemorrhage; gastrointestinal bleeding; liver injury (ALT more than three times the upper limit).
record.full_text_note: The full text reports major bleeding, intracranial haemorrhage and gastrointestinal bleeding with numbers. Clinically relevant non-major bleeding and liver injury are not reported anywhere in the article or its supplement. No explanation is given.
record.regulatory_summary_excerpt: A regulator's public assessment report (fictional) for ZX-44 notes: 'Hepatic laboratory data from ZEPHYR-AF were reviewed. The committee considered the hepatic safety profile acceptable and recommended routine liver monitoring in the product information.' No numbers are given in the public report.
record.funding: Sponsored by the manufacturer of ZX-44, which designed the trial, held the data and drafted the manuscript with the academic steering committee.
record.author_contact: The review team emailed the corresponding author requesting the missing outcomes. The sponsor replied that the data are 'available through the company's data-sharing portal after approval of a research proposal', which typically takes three to six months.
record.steering_committee_letter: In a later letter to the journal, two academic members of the steering committee wrote that clinically relevant non-major bleeding had been 'analysed and discussed' by the committee and was 'broadly similar between groups', and that liver enzyme elevations were 'uncommon and balanced'. They said the omission from the paper reflected 'space constraints' and that the sponsor had agreed to post the full safety tables on the registry, which had not happened at the time of the review's search.
